    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # A is updated in-place during Gram–Schmidt and also printed at the end.
    # Access pattern is almost exclusively column-wise: A[:, k], A[:, j].
    # Use column-major layout so inner i-loops are unit-stride.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i  # column-major

    # R is upper triangular; we mostly access rows R[k, k..N-1].
    # Keep row-major so R[k, *] is unit-stride in j.
    R[k, j]: out DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j    # row-major

    # Q stores orthonormal columns Q[:, k]; always accessed column-wise.
    # Use same column-major layout as A.
    Q[i, j]: out DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i    # column-major

    # Scalar temporaries, live only inside one k-iteration at a time.
    nrm:    temp DATA_TYPE
    inv_rkk: temp DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    M: int          # problem height (rows of A, Q)
    N: int          # problem width  (cols of A, Q and R)
    TI: int         # optional tile size for i (rows), tuning parameter
    TJ: int         # tile size for j (trailing columns), tuning parameter
    VF: int         # vectorization factor along i (rows), e.g., SIMD width
    UF: int         # unroll factor for innermost i-loops

computation:
    # Modified Gram–Schmidt QR factorization:
    # for k = 0..N-1:
    #   1) R[k,k] = ||A[:,k]||_2
    #   2) Q[:,k] = A[:,k] / R[k,k]
    #   3) For each j>k:
    #        R[k,j] = Q[:,k]^T * A[:,j]
    #        A[:,j] = A[:,j] - Q[:,k] * R[k,j]

    K_LOOP:
      for k in seq([0, N)):                # k must be sequential

        # 1) Squared 2-norm of k-th column of A
        NORM_COL:
          nrm = SCALAR_VAL(0.0)
          nrm = nrm + sum(i, A[i, k] * A[i, k])

        # 2) Normalize column k to obtain Q[:,k] and diagonal R[k,k]
        R_DIAG:
          R[k, k] = SQRT_FUN(nrm)
        RECIP_R_DIAG:
          # Precompute reciprocal once per k:
          # replaces M divisions with M multiplications.
          inv_rkk = SCALAR_VAL(1.0) / R[k, k]
        NORMALIZE_Q_COL:
          for i:
            Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * inv_rkk

        # 3) Orthogonalize remaining columns j > k against Q[:,k]
        ORTHO_TRAILING:
          for j in [k + 1, N):
            DOT_INIT:
              R[k, j] = SCALAR_VAL(0.0)
            DOT_PRODUCT:
              # R[k,j] = Q[:,k]^T * A[:,j]
              R[k, j] = R[k, j] + sum(i, Q[i, k] * A[i, j])
            UPDATE_TRAILING_COL:
              # A[:,j] -= Q[:,k] * R[k,j]
              for i:
                A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

optimization:
    # Layout choices:
    # - A and Q in column-major (already encoded in 'data') so
    #   inner loops over i access contiguous memory (A[i,k], A[i,j], Q[i,k]).
    # - R in row-major so R[k, j] is contiguous in j and cache-friendly.

    # Tiling in the trailing-column dimension j:
    # - For each k, we process columns j in blocks of size TJ.
    # - Each block corresponds to a compact submatrix A[:, J] and row slice R[k, J].
    # - This improves cache locality and gives coarse-grain units for parallel work.
    block(j, J, TJ)

    # Optional tiling in the row dimension i:
    # - Implemented with partial reductions over tiles for the dot products.
    # - Keeps slices of A[:, *] and Q[:, k] in L1/L2.
    # - Must preserve reduction semantics for nrm and R[k, j].
    block(i, I, TI)

    # Parallelization:
    # - k-loop remains sequential (true data dependence: each k updates A[:, j>k]).
    # - For fixed k, different trailing columns j>k are independent:
    #   each uses Q[:,k] read-only and disjoint A[:,j], R[k,j].
    # - Parallelize the J-tiles of j inside ORTHO_TRAILING.
    parallelize(J)

    # Vectorization and unrolling:
    # - All innermost i-loops (norm, normalization, dot products,
    #   and A-updates) traverse i with unit stride due to column-major layout.
    # - Vectorize over i to exploit SIMD, and unroll to reduce loop overhead.
    vectorize(i, VF)
    unroll(i, UF)

data:
    # Row-major layout (PolyBench default): element (i, j) is stored at i * N + j
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    Q[i, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    R[i, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Temporary: inverse of the column norm, one scalar per k.
    inv_rkk[k]: temp DATA_TYPE = (k) -> k

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters (compile-time or runtime constants)
    T_i: int  # tile size for row dimension i (e.g., 128 or 256)
    T_j: int  # tile size for column dimension j>k (e.g., 32 or 64)
    V_i: int  # SIMD width for vectorization along i (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 4 for double)
    U_i: int  # unroll factor for inner i loops

computation:
    # Outer loop over columns (k): modified Gram–Schmidt
    for k in seq([0, N)):
        # 1. Compute squared 2-norm of k-th column of A.
        nrm_k:
            nrm = sum(i in [0, M)) (A[i, k] * A[i, k])

        # 2. Normalize k-th column and write Q[:,k] and R[k,k].
        normalize_k:
            R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm)
            inv_rkk[k] = 1.0 / R[k, k]
            for i in [0, M):
                Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * inv_rkk[k]

        # 3. Initialize R[k, j] for trailing columns j > k.
        init_R_row_k:
            for j in [k + 1, N):
                R[k, j] = 0.0

        # 4. Build R[k, j] = <Q[:,k], A[:,j]> for all j>k.
        #    Loop order (i outer, j inner) gives row-wise traversal of A,
        #    improving cache locality for the large M×(N−k−1) trailing panel.
        build_R_row_k:
            for i in [0, M):
                qki = Q[i, k]
                for j in [k + 1, N):
                    R[k, j] += qki * A[i, j]

        # 5. Make remaining columns orthogonal to q_k:
        #       A[:,j] = A[:,j] − q_k * R[k,j],  for all j>k.
        #    Again use row-wise traversal of A for good locality.
        update_trailing_cols:
            for i in [0, M):
                qki = Q[i, k]
                for j in [k + 1, N):
                    A[i, j] = A[i, j] - qki * R[k, j]

optimization:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Arithmetic simplification: remove M divisions per column
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Original:
    #   nrm = sum_i A[i,k]^2
    #   R[k,k] = sqrt(nrm)
    #   Q[i,k] = A[i,k] / R[k,k]
    #
    # Optimized (as modeled above):
    #   nrm      = sum_i A[i,k]^2
    #   R[k,k]   = sqrt(nrm)
    #   inv_rkk  = 1 / R[k,k]
    #   Q[i,k]   = A[i,k] * inv_rkk
    #
    # This replaces M divisions per k by one division plus M multiplications,
    # preserving the mathematical result R[k,k] = ||A[:,k]||_2 and
    # Q[:,k] = A[:,k] / R[k,k].

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Loop restructuring and blocking for the trailing update (steps 4 & 5)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The expensive part of the algorithm is the work on the trailing panel
    # A[:, j>k] in build_R_row_k and update_trailing_cols. We:
    #   - traverse A row-wise (i outer, j inner) to make accesses to A[i,j]
    #     contiguous in memory (row-major layout),
    #   - tile both i and j to improve cache reuse and enable parallelism.
    #
    # Tiling is applied only to the doubly-nested (i, j) loops in
    # build_R_row_k and update_trailing_cols.
    block(i, I, T_i)      # Split i into outer tile index I and inner i.
    block(j, J, T_j)      # Split j>k into outer tile index J and inner j.

    # After blocking, the relevant parts conceptually look like:
    #   for k:
    #     ...
    #     for J:
    #       # columns j in tile J, j ∈ [k+1, N)
    #       for I:
    #         for i in tile I:
    #           qki = Q[i,k]
    #           for j in tile J:
    #             R[k,j] += qki * A[i,j]
    #     for J:
    #       for I:
    #         for i in tile I:
    #           qki = Q[i,k]
    #           for j in tile J:
    #             A[i,j] -= qki * R[k,j]

    # Hoist tile loops so that tiles (J, then I) become outer around the
    # inner i and j loops in steps 4 and 5. This exposes coarse-grain
    # parallelism and improves temporal locality on R[k, j] and A[i, j].
    hoist(J)
    hoist(I)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelism
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The outer k-loop is inherently sequential: column k+1 depends on the
    # updated A, Q, and R from column k. We therefore do NOT parallelize k.
    #
    # Within a given k, however, different trailing columns j>k are
    # independent. After tiling, each J tile corresponds to an independent
    # block of columns {j}, so we safely parallelize across J for both
    # build_R_row_k and update_trailing_cols.
    parallelize(J)   # e.g., OpenMP parallel for over J inside each fixed k.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization and unrolling
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Inner loops along i operate on rows of A with j fixed within a tile,
    # so A[i,j] is contiguous in memory. qki is a scalar broadcast, making
    # the following idioms SIMD-friendly:
    #   R[k,j] += qki * A[i,j]
    #   A[i,j] -= qki * R[k,j]
    #
    # We therefore:
    vectorize(i, V_i)     # Vectorize inner i-loops in steps 4 and 5.
    unroll(i, U_i)        # Unroll the same i-loops to increase ILP.

    # On a modern x64 with wide SIMD (e.g., AVX2/AVX-512), typical choices:
    #   - V_i ≈ hardware SIMD width (e.g., 4 for double, 8 for float),
    #   - U_i chosen so that V_i * U_i keeps the register file busy without
    #     causing spills.

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Cache-aware tile size selection
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Choose T_i and T_j so that one (I, J) tile of A and R fits comfortably
    # in L1 or L2 cache:
    #   T_i * T_j * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)  (for A)
    # + T_j * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)       (for R[k, j] row)
    # is well below the target cache size.
    #
    # Example for double precision on a typical x64:
    #   - T_i in [128, 256]
    #   - T_j in [32, 64]
    #
    # No additional large buffers are introduced: only the inv_rkk[k] array
    # (O(N) scalars), which is negligible relative to the O(MN) storage of A
    # and Q and stays well within the 50% memory overhead budget.

domain:
    # Matrix dimensions (as in the C code: M rows, N columns)
    i: dim in [0, M)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index
    k: dim in [0, N)          # Gram–Schmidt step / column index

data:
    # A: input matrix, overwritten in-place during Gram–Schmidt
    # Layout kept row-major to favor the heavy i,j-nested phases which
    # traverse A row-wise.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j      # M×N, row-major

    # Q: orthonormal basis; accessed and written mostly column-wise,
    # so we flip it to column-major to make accesses Q[i,k] contiguous.
    Q[i, j]: out  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i       # M×N, column-major

    # R: upper-triangular factor; accessed row-wise (R[k, j] for fixed k),
    # so we keep it row-major.
    R[i, j]: out  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j       # N×N, row-major

    # Temporary: reciprocal of the diagonal entries of R, one per column.
    # This lets us replace M divisions per column by M multiplications.
    invR[k]: temp DATA_TYPE = k                         # 1D, contiguous

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (as in the C code)
    M: int
    N: int

    # Tuning parameters for the optimized schedule (chosen empirically)
    TI: int      # optional tile size in i (rows)  – may be unused or set to 0
    TJ: int      # tile size in j (columns), e.g., 64 or 128
    TVEC: int    # SIMD width in elements along j, e.g., 4 or 8
    NTHREADS: int  # maximum number of worker threads used for parallel tiles

computation:
    # Modified Gram–Schmidt QR factorization (mathematically identical to the C code).
    # We keep the outer k-loop sequential because each step uses the updated A from
    # previous steps.

    for k in seq[0, N):                          # sequential over k

        # 1) Compute squared 2-norm of column k of A and the diagonal R[k,k].
        #    This matches:
        #      nrm = 0; for i: nrm += A[i][k]*A[i][k]; R[k][k] = sqrt(nrm);

        NORM[k]:
            let nrm_k = sum(i in [0, M)) (A[i, k] * A[i, k])
            R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm_k)

        # 1b) Precompute reciprocal of R[k,k] to avoid M divisions in the
        #     normalization step. This is algebraically:
        #       invR[k] = 1.0 / R[k,k];
        #       Q[i,k] = A[i,k] * invR[k];   (instead of A[i,k] / R[k,k])

        INV_R[k]:
            invR[k] = 1.0 / R[k, k]

        # 2) Normalize k-th column of A into Q:
        #       for i: Q[i][k] = A[i][k] / R[k][k];
        #    replaced by multiplication with invR[k].

        NORMALIZE_Q[k]:
            for i in [0, M):
                Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * invR[k]

        # 3) Compute the k-th row of R to the right of the diagonal, i.e.
        #       for j > k: R[k][j] = sum_i Q[i,k] * A[i,j]
        #
        # To improve cache locality, we evaluate this row as:
        #   - first initialize R[k,j] = 0 for j>k,
        #   - then perform a matrix–vector-like accumulation over i,j:
        #       for i: for j>k: R[k,j] += Q[i,k] * A[i,j]
        #
        # This is mathematically equivalent to doing the dot-products
        # column-by-column, but allows row-wise traversal of A and R,
        # which is more cache friendly.

        INIT_R_ROW[k]:
            for j in [0, N):
                if j > k:
                    R[k, j] = 0.0

        ACCUM_R_ROW[k]:
            for i in [0, M):
                for j in [0, N):
                    if j > k:
                        R[k, j] += Q[i, k] * A[i, j]

        # 4) Update trailing columns of A using the just-computed R[k, j]:
        #       for j > k: for i: A[i][j] -= Q[i][k] * R[k][j]
        #
        # We apply this as a 2D sweep over (i,j) with j as the fast dimension,
        # so both A[i,j] (row-major) and R[k,j] (row-major) are accessed
        # contiguously in memory.

        UPDATE_A[k]:
            for i in [0, M):
                for j in [0, N):
                    if j > k:
                        A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

dependencies:
    # Intra-k dependencies (must be respected for each fixed k):
    for k in [0, N):
        NORM[k]      -> INV_R[k]
        INV_R[k]     -> NORMALIZE_Q[k]
        NORMALIZE_Q[k] -> INIT_R_ROW[k]
        INIT_R_ROW[k]  -> ACCUM_R_ROW[k]
        ACCUM_R_ROW[k] -> UPDATE_A[k]

    # Inter-k dependency: each step k+1 must see A already updated by step k.
    for k in [0, N-1):
        UPDATE_A[k] -> NORM[k+1]

optimization:
    #---------------------------------------
    # 1. Arithmetic simplification
    #---------------------------------------
    # We already introduced invR[k] in the computation. Conceptually this is:
    #   - For each k: compute invR[k] = 1.0 / R[k,k] once.
    #   - Replace Q[i,k] = A[i,k] / R[k,k] with a cheaper multiply:
    #       Q[i,k] = A[i,k] * invR[k].
    #
    # This reduces the cost of normalization from O(M) divisions to
    # O(1) division + O(M) multiplications per column.

    # (No extra directive needed; this optimization is fully encoded
    #  in the computation section via invR.)

    #---------------------------------------
    # 2. Data layout optimization
    #---------------------------------------
    # Q is made column-major (see data section), which:
    #   - makes writes to Q[i,k] in NORMALIZE_Q[k] contiguous in memory,
    #   - improves reuse in ACCUM_R_ROW and UPDATE_A because Q[i,k] is
    #     read in a pure i-loop and can be streamed.
    #
    # A and R remain row-major to favor the heavy i,j sweeps, which
    # traverse rows with j as the innermost dimension.

    #---------------------------------------
    # 3. Loop blocking and SIMD vectorization over j
    #---------------------------------------
    # The dominant cost is in ACCUM_R_ROW[k] and UPDATE_A[k]:
    #   both are O(M * N^2) operations, traversing submatrices of A and
    #   rows of R. We block and vectorize along j to:
    #     - improve cache locality for A[i,j] and R[k,j],
    #     - exploit SIMD on the innermost j-loop.
    #
    # We split j into tiles of size TJ:
    #   j = J * TJ + j_inner, with 0 <= j_inner < TJ.
    #
    # This applies to all loops that use j as a spatial dimension
    # (INIT_R_ROW, ACCUM_R_ROW, UPDATE_A).

    block(j, J, TJ)          # tile the column dimension into J (tile index) and j (in-tile index)

    # Within each tile, j is the innermost loop, so it is a natural SIMD
    # target. TVEC should match or divide the hardware vector width.

    vectorize(j, TVEC)       # SIMD vectorization over contiguous columns j within a tile

    #---------------------------------------
    # 4. Parallelization over independent column tiles
    #---------------------------------------
    # For a fixed k, different columns j > k are independent:
    #   - ACCUM_R_ROW[k]: each R[k,j] depends only on Q[:,k] and A[:,j].
    #   - UPDATE_A[k]:    each A[:,j] is updated with Q[:,k] and R[k,j].
    # After tiling, each J-tile touches a disjoint set of columns, so we
    # can process these tiles in parallel without synchronization.
    #
    # We exploit this by parallelizing over the tile index J in all
    # j-tiled loops (INIT_R_ROW, ACCUM_R_ROW, UPDATE_A).

    parallelize(J)           # parallel tiles of columns, up to NTHREADS workers

    #---------------------------------------
    # 5. Local scalar reuse and unrolling over i
    #---------------------------------------
    # In ACCUM_R_ROW and UPDATE_A, Q[i,k] is reused across all j in the
    # innermost loop. Compilers will typically hoist this into a register.
    # We additionally suggest modest unrolling of the i-loop to increase
    # instruction-level parallelism (ILP), especially when M is large.

    unroll(i, 4)             # unroll row-iterations to improve ILP where profitable

    #---------------------------------------
    # 6. Optional: outer-k scheduling
    #---------------------------------------
    # The k-loop is inherently sequential due to the dependence
    # UPDATE_A[k] -> NORM[k+1], so we do NOT parallelize k.
    # However, k is hoisted as the outermost loop (as in the C code),
    # which:
    #   - maximizes reuse of a single column Q[:,k] and row R[k,*]
    #     across the inner i,j sweeps,
    #   - minimizes working set size per step.

    hoist(k)                 # keep k as the outermost loop (already implied by computation)

    # A is updated in-place and used as workspace during Gram–Schmidt.
    # Store A in column-major order so that inner loops over i access
    # contiguous memory (better cache + SIMD).
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i    # column-major

    # Q holds the orthonormal basis vectors (columns); it is filled by the kernel.
    # Same column-major layout as A, for contiguous access along i.
    Q[i, j]: out  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i     # column-major

    # R is upper-triangular; row-major is natural because we traverse rows R[k, j]
    # for fixed k and varying j.
    R[i, j]: out  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j     # row-major

    # nrm[k]:   temporary DATA_TYPE   # column squared norms
    # Rinv[k]:  temporary DATA_TYPE   # 1 / R[k, k] to replace divisions by multiplies

parameters:
    # Tuning knobs, chosen based on cache / SIMD characteristics of the target.
    TILE_M: int    # tile size along i (rows), e.g., 128
    TILE_N: int    # tile size along j (columns), e.g., 32
    VEC_WIDTH: int # SIMD width in elements (e.g., 4 for double on AVX2)
    NUM_THREADS: int  # maximum number of worker threads for parallel regions

computation:
    # Modified Gram–Schmidt (MGS) QR factorization of A:
    # for each column k, build Q[:,k] and the k-th row of R, and update
    # the trailing columns of A.

    for k in seq([0, N)):
        # 1. Compute squared 2-norm of k-th column of current A, and R[k, k].
        R_diag[k]:
            R[k, k] = sqrt( sum(i in [0, M)) (A[i, k] * A[i, k]) )

        # 2. Normalize k-th column to obtain Q[:, k].
        NORM_Q[k]:
            for i in [0, M):
                Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k]

        # 3. For each trailing column j > k, compute R[k, j] as
        #    R[k, j] = Q[:,k]^T * A[:,j].
        R_ROW[k]:
            for j in [k+1, N):
                R[k, j] = sum(i in [0, M)) (Q[i, k] * A[i, j])

        # 4. Update trailing columns of A by removing their projection on Q[:,k]:
        #    A[:, j] <- A[:, j] - R[k, j] * Q[:, k] for j > k.
        UPDATE_A[k]:
            for j in [k+1, N):
                for i in [0, M):
                    A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

dependencies:
    # Within a given k, the four phases are ordered:
    for k in [0, N):
        R_diag(k)  -> NORM_Q(k)
        NORM_Q(k)  -> R_ROW(k)
        R_ROW(k)   -> UPDATE_A(k)

    # Between different k, all work for step k must complete before step k+1 starts,
    # because A and Q produced at step k are inputs to all later steps.
    for k in [0, N-1):
        UPDATE_A(k) -> R_diag(k+1)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Data layout and scalar-strength reduction

    #  - improves spatial locality for A[:, j] and Q[:, k]

    #   and rewrites:
    #     Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k]

    #     Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * Rinv[k]

    #
    # block(i, ii, TILE_M) rewrites loops over i as:
    #   for ii in [0, ceil(M / TILE_M)):
    #     for i in [ii*TILE_M, min((ii+1)*TILE_M, M)):
    #       ...
    block(i, ii, TILE_M)

    # For the trailing matrix operations (R_ROW and UPDATE_A), also tile
    # columns (j) so that each worker operates on a submatrix A[*, j_block]
    # that better fits cache.
    #
    # block(j, jj, TILE_N) rewrites loops over j as:
    #   for jj in [0, ceil(N / TILE_N)):
    #     for j in [jj*TILE_N, min((jj+1)*TILE_N, N)):
    #       ...
    block(j, jj, TILE_N)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelization
    #------------------------------------------------------------

    # 1) Column norm and normalization (per k):
    #    - Norm is a reduction over i.
    #    - Normalization is embarrassingly parallel over i.
    #
    # We parallelize over the outer i-tiles (ii) for these phases, using
    # a reduction on the norm in R_diag and a plain parallel for in NORM_Q.

    # Parallelize tiled rows for norm computation with reduction on the scalar
    # R[k, k] (or equivalently on the intermediate norm).
    #
    # #reduction(R[k, k], +) indicates that updates to the running norm are
    # privatized per thread and combined with a sum at the end.
    parallelize(ii) in R_diag
    #reduction(R[k, k], +)

    # Parallelize normalization across row-tiles; each iteration writes distinct
    # elements Q[i, k] and reads shared scalars A[i, k], R[k, k].
    parallelize(ii) in NORM_Q

    # 2) Trailing matrix operations R_ROW and UPDATE_A:
    #    For fixed k, different columns j > k are independent. We parallelize
    #    over column tiles jj, which gives coarse-grained tasks and avoids
    #    reductions across threads.
    #
    #    Within each column tile, j and i remain purely loop-level parallel
    #    (no cross-iteration dependencies), but they will be executed
    #    sequentially within a thread to keep synchronization overhead low.

    parallelize(jj) in R_ROW
    parallelize(jj) in UPDATE_A

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization and unrolling
    #------------------------------------------------------------

    # Vectorize inner loops over i (rows) where data is contiguous
    # thanks to column-major layout:
    #  - in R_diag: loads/stores on A[i, k]
    #  - in NORM_Q: loads A[i, k] and stores Q[i, k]
    #  - in R_ROW: loads Q[i, k] and A[i, j]
    #  - in UPDATE_A: loads/stores A[i, j] and loads Q[i, k], R[k, j]
    #
    # vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) expresses that the compiler should generate
    # SIMD instructions processing VEC_WIDTH consecutive i-values per step.
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) in R_diag
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) in NORM_Q
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) in R_ROW
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH) in UPDATE_A

    # Unroll the innermost i-loops by a small factor to expose more ILP
    # and reduce loop overhead without blowing up code size.
    unroll(i, 4) in R_diag
    unroll(i, 4) in NORM_Q
    unroll(i, 4) in R_ROW
    unroll(i, 4) in UPDATE_A

    # Modified Gram–Schmidt, column by column.
    # k is explicitly sequential because each step depends on updates to A and R from previous k.
    K_LOOP:
    for k in seq([0, N)):
        # 1) Compute the 2-norm of column k of the current A and store it on the diagonal of R.
        R_DIAG:
            R[k, k] = sqrt( sum(i in [0, M), A[i, k] * A[i, k]) )

        # 2) Normalize column k of A to obtain column k of Q.
        Q_COL:
            for i in [0, M):
                Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k]

        # 3a) Initialize the upper-triangular part of row k of R for columns j > k.
        R_ROW_INIT:
            for j in [k + 1, N):
                R[k, j] = 0.0

        # 3b) Compute row k of R:
        #     For each j > k, R[k,j] = sum_i Q[i,k] * A[i,j].
        #     Loops are organized with i outer, j inner to make A’s row-major layout contiguous in j.
        R_ROW_ACC:
            for i in [0, M):
                for j in [k + 1, N):
                    R[k, j] = R[k, j] + Q[i, k] * A[i, j]

        # 4) Orthogonalize the remaining columns of A against Q[:,k]:
        #    A[:,j] ← A[:,j] − Q[:,k] * R[k,j] for all j > k.
        #    Same i-outer, j-inner order for good row-major locality.
        A_UPDATE:
            for i in [0, M):
                for j in [k + 1, N):
                    A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

dependencies:
    # k must remain sequential: later columns depend on the updated A and R from earlier k.
    for k in [0, N - 1]:

    #   - R_ROW_INIT and R_ROW_ACC produce R[k,j] for j > k
    #   - A_UPDATE consumes those R[k,j] and the updated Q[:,k]

optimization:

    block(i, ii, I_BLOCK)      # i = ii * I_BLOCK + i_inner
    block(j, jj, J_BLOCK)      # j = jj * J_BLOCK + j_inner
